data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's adversarial-perturbation design cannot satisfy its own success criterion. It states perturbations should 'modify inputs to satisfy checklist items without altering the ground-truth outcome.' But the problem asks for tasks 'with objectively verifiable outcomes' where the checklist is supposed to be a causal proxy for those outcomes. If the perturbation must leave the objective outcome unchanged while changing features the checklist uses as causal proxies, then either (a) the checklist items are genuinely causal for the outcome, in which case perturbing them necessarily changes the outcome — making the perturbation impossible — or (b) the checklist items are non-causal, in which case 'satisfying checklist items' without changing the outcome is trivially achievable by swapping one non-causal surface feature for another, but that only tests whether the panel rigidly keys on that specific surface feature; it does not distinguish a checklist that causally tracks the right answer from one that merely complies with a different but equally non-causal surface proxy. SRC_001's countercondition (perfect causal completeness) concedes the impossibility for the genuine-gain case, undermining the test's applicability exactly when the target claim most needs to demonstrate genuine gain.
